Interviewer: "When would you use DynamoDB vs a relational database?" — literally every AWS interview lol


DynamoDB's your pick when you need crazy scale, fast reads/writes, and don't mind a schema-less vibe. It's NoSQL so no complex joins. Perfect for stuff like user sessions, IoT data, or anything with unpredictable traffic spikes. RDS is better when you've got complex queries, need ACID transactions, or your data's relational (think ecommerce with orders → items → customers). DynamoDB costs more at small scale but destroys RDS at massive throughput. Know your access patterns before picking one.

Interviewer: "What's the difference between Docker and Podman?" — loads of people think they're basically the same thing


So Docker uses a daemon (background service running as root) that manages containers. Podman? Daemonless. You run containers directly without needing root privileges, which is a big security win. Both use the same image format so switching isn't painful.

Gotcha: Podman's still catching up on some ecosystem stuff. Docker's just more mature and widely used in prod right now. But Podman's definitely gaining traction, especially for rootless deployments.

Interviewer: "How do you handle encryption keys in the cloud? Should you manage them yourself or use a service like KMS?" — literally every security round


Honestly, manage them yourself and you're asking for trouble. KMS (or similar) handles rotation, access control, and audit logs automatically. You just call it when you need to encrypt/decrypt. Plus if someone gets your app server, they don't have the keys — they're locked in a separate service. That separation is the whole point. Self-managing keys is fine for learning but in prod? Use the service. It's not worth the risk.

Interviewer: "What's the difference between a service mesh and just using Kubernetes services?" — honestly this trips people up



K8s services handle basic routing and load balancing within the cluster. A service mesh like Istio sits on top and gives you way more — traffic management, circuit breakers, retries, distributed tracing, mTLS encryption between services, canary deployments. It's like K8s services are your basic networking, but Istio is your sophisticated traffic control center. Catch: Istio adds complexity and latency, so don't reach for it unless you actually need those features. Most teams start simple with K8s services first.

Interviewer: "When would you use Step Functions instead of just throwing everything in a Lambda?" — honestly this one trips people up


Step Functions are for workflows that need multiple steps, error handling, and retries across different services. Like if you're processing an order — validate payment, check inventory, send confirmation email, update database. Each step might fail differently. Lambda has a 15 min timeout, but Step Functions can run for days. Plus you get built-in retry logic and dead letter queues. Single Lambda doing all that? Recipe for disaster.

Gotcha: people think Step Functions are overkill for simple stuff. They're not. But if it's just "call one API and return the result" yeah, Lambda alone is fine.

#AWS #StepFunctions #Serverless #CloudArchitecture #DevOpsInterview

Interviewer: "What's a buildpack and why would you use one instead of writing a Dockerfile?"

Lol this trips people up. A buildpack is basically a script that detects your app type and builds it for you. No Dockerfile needed.

You push your code. The buildpack sees "oh this is Node.js" and automatically installs dependencies, sets up the runtime, and packages it. Done.

Docker forces you to write every step. Buildpacks just... figure it out.

Where they shine: platforms like Heroku and Cloud Foundry. You literally just git push and it works. Great for teams that don't want DevOps overhead.

Downside: less control. If you need custom stuff, you might need to write your own buildpack or just use Docker.

Real talk: startups and small teams love buildpacks. Enterprise shops usually stick with Docker because they want total control.

Interviewer: "What's Infrastructure as Code and why do we use it?"

Good question. It's writing code that builds your servers and cloud stuff instead of clicking buttons in the AWS console.

Instead of manually creating 50 servers, you write code that says "make 50 servers with these settings." Then you run it. Done. And you can run it again whenever you want. Same result every time.

Why this matters: You can version control it (Git). You can review changes before applying them. You can copy your setup to a new team or environment super fast. No more "wait, how did we set this up last time?"

Tools like Pulumi, Terraform, and CloudFormation all do this. They're just different ways to write the recipe for your infrastructure.

Real example: Instead of clicking to create a database, subnet, and firewall rule, you write 10 lines of code. One command deploys all three. Your coworker can read it and understand your setup immediately.

#DevOps #InfrastructureAsCode #AWS #CloudArchitecture

Interviewer: "What's the difference between monitoring and observability? Why does it matter?"

Ngl, a lot of people mix these up.

Monitoring = checking specific things. You pick what to watch. Metrics, logs, alerts. You're looking for what you expect to break.

Observability = being able to ask ANY question about your system. Why is this slow? Where did that error come from? What happened 5 minutes ago? You don't need to predict it first.

Real example: You monitor CPU and memory. But your app is slow and you don't know why. With observability, you can dig into traces and see exactly which database query is hanging.

Istio (a service mesh) helps with observability. It watches traffic between services automatically. You get timing, errors, and flow without changing your app code.

The key: monitoring catches what you're looking for. Observability lets you find what you didn't expect to break.

#SRE #Observability #DevOps #Monitoring #Istio

Interviewer: "How do you monitor a Step Function workflow? What would you watch for?"

This one trips people up ngl


Step Functions run tasks in order. You need to watch:

1. Execution status - is it running, done, or stuck?
2. How long each step takes - one step getting slow? Investigate.
3. Failed executions - did a step error out?
4. CloudWatch Logs - what did your code actually do?

The key: set alarms. If executions fail too much, alert your team NOW. Don't wait for customers to complain.

Real example: Your Step Function calls a Lambda. Lambda times out. You catch this with CloudWatch Metrics + alarms. Fix it before it breaks production.

Also watch execution history. Sometimes a workflow fails silently. The logs tell the story.

#SRE #AWS #StepFunctions #Observability #DevOps

Interviewer: "How do you let your app in Kubernetes talk to AWS without storing secret keys in your code?"

Ngl, this trips people up. But it's actually smart.


You use IRSA. That's just a fancy name for: your pod gets a temporary ID from AWS. No keys sitting around.

Here's how it works:
1. You create an AWS role (like a permission ticket)
2. You link it to your Kubernetes service account
3. When your pod starts, AWS gives it temp keys that expire
4. Your app uses those keys. No hardcoding secrets.

Why this matters: if someone hacks your pod, they only get temp keys that expire in an hour. Not your main AWS keys forever.

Real example: Your app needs to read from S3. Instead of putting AWS keys in your deployment, IRSA handles it. Your pod just asks AWS "can I read this bucket?" AWS checks the role and says yes or no.

It's basically: "prove who you are" instead of "here's my password."

#Kubernetes #AWS #DevOps #SRE #InterviewPrep

Interviewer: "How do you monitor network traffic in your VPC? What would you check if users say the app is slow?"

Ngl, this trips people up because they mix up monitoring with just "checking logs"

You'd look at:

1. VPC Flow Logs - see what packets are moving where. Spot blocked traffic or weird patterns.

2. CloudWatch metrics - CPU, memory, network in/out. If network out is maxed, you found your problem.

3. Check your security groups - maybe you're blocking traffic by accident. Or a route is wrong.

4. Look at NAT gateway/instance - if everyone's going through one box, it becomes a bottleneck.

Real example: User says "slow". You check Flow Logs, see traffic hitting a security group deny rule. You're rejecting it! Fix the rule, boom, problem solved.

The key: start at the network layer first. Don't jump straight to app logs.

#DevOps #AWS #SRE #InterviewTips #Monitoring

Interviewer: "You deploy a Lambda function. It runs fine in dev but times out in prod. How do you debug this?"

Lol this one's tricky because you can't just SSH in.


First: check CloudWatch logs. Look for actual errors or slow queries. Lambda logs everything there.

Second: check your timeout setting. Maybe it's set too low for prod traffic.

Third: is it a cold start? First run takes longer. Use provisioned concurrency to keep Lambdas warm.

Fourth: check what your function actually does. Database queries slow? API calls hanging? Memory too low? All of these slow things down.

Pro tip: add CloudWatch metrics to track execution time. You'll see patterns. Like "it only times out when database is busy." That tells you where to look.

Real example: I once had a Lambda that was fine with 128MB memory in dev but needed 512MB in prod because of data volume. Just didn't have enough resources to work fast.

#DevOps #AWS #Lambda #SRE #Observability

Interviewer: "What's the difference between logs, metrics, and traces? Why do you need all three?"

Ngl, this trips people up but it's actually simple.

Logs are messages your app writes. "User logged in at 3:45pm." Raw text.

Metrics are numbers over time. "5 requests per second." "CPU at 80%." You graph these.

Traces follow one request through your whole system. "Request hit API, then database, took 200ms total." Shows you where slowness happens.

Why all three? Logs tell you WHAT happened. Metrics tell you IF something's wrong. Traces tell you WHERE it broke.

Real example: Your app is slow. Metrics show "yeah, something's up." Logs say "database connection failed." Traces show the request waited 5 seconds at the database step. Now you know exactly what to fix.

Build observability into your infrastructure from day one. Use Pulumi or Terraform to set up monitoring with your apps. Don't add it later.

#SRE #Observability #DevOps #Monitoring #InterviewPrep

Interviewer: "What's the difference between SNS and SQS? When do you use each one?"

This one trips people up ngl


SNS is a megaphone. You shout a message once, and everyone listening hears it right away. Good for alerts, notifications, stuff that needs to go to lots of places fast.

SQS is a mailbox. Messages sit there until someone grabs them. Great when you need to queue up work, handle spiky traffic, or make sure nothing gets lost.

Key diff: SNS = push (send and forget). SQS = pull (grab when ready).

Example: Your app crashes. Use SNS to alert your team NOW. But if you need to process 10k orders today, throw them in SQS so workers can grab them one at a time without getting slammed.

Bonus: you can actually send SNS messages TO SQS queues. They work great together.

#AWS #DevOps #InterviewPrep #CloudArchitecture

Interviewer: "You're running containers in ECS. How do you keep your app safe from the internet?"

Ngl this trips people up but it's pretty straightforward.

You use security groups. Think of them like a bouncer at a club. They say: "Yeah, traffic on port 80 can come in. Port 22? Nah, not today."

ECS containers run inside a VPC (your private network). By default, nothing from the internet can reach them. You only open the ports you need.

The setup:
- Create a security group for your ECS tasks
- Allow port 80/443 for web traffic (from anywhere)
- Block everything else
- Attach it to your load balancer in front

The load balancer sits in public. Your containers hide behind it and the security group.

Pro tip: Don't open port 22 (SSH) to 0.0.0.0. That's asking for trouble. Use AWS Systems Manager Session Manager instead—it's way safer.

#ECS #AWS #DevOps #SecurityGroups #InterviewPrep

Interviewer: "Why can't my Docker container talk to another container on the same machine?"

This trips people up all the time lol


By default, Docker containers can't see each other. Each one gets its own isolated network. They're like roommates in separate boxes.

You have two options:

1. **Docker networks** — create a custom network and put both containers on it. They can talk by container name. This is the right way.

2. **Host network** — the container uses your machine's network directly. Fast but loses isolation. Not great for security.

Real example: if your app container needs to hit a database container, put them both on the same custom network. Then use the database container's name as the hostname. That's it.

Most people forget about custom networks and try to hardcode IP addresses. Don't do that — IPs change.

#Docker #DevOps #Networking #InterviewTips #Containerization

Interviewer: "How do you store secrets like passwords and API keys? Why can't we just put them in code?"

ngl this trips up a lot of people


You never put secrets in your code. Ever. Because:

1. If your code goes on GitHub, hackers find them in 5 seconds
2. Everyone on your team sees them (bad idea)
3. You can't change them without redeploying code

Instead, use a secrets manager like HashiCorp Vault or AWS Secrets Manager.

How it works:
- Your app asks the vault "hey, give me the database password"
- Vault checks if the app is allowed to have it
- Vault gives it only when needed
- You can rotate passwords without touching code

Real example: Your app running on a server needs a DB password. Instead of hardcoding it, the server talks to Vault at startup. Vault says "ok, here's your password for the next hour." After an hour? Vault stops accepting that password. The server asks again. New password. Way safer.

#DevOps #Security #CloudSecurity #Vault #Secrets

Interviewer: "Walk me through what happens when you configure a firewall rule. Why does order matter?"

ohh this trips people up


A firewall reads rules from top to bottom. It stops at the first match. So order = everything.

Example: You have two rules:
1. Block port 22 (SSH)
2. Allow port 22 from 10.0.0.0/8

If rule 1 is first? SSH gets blocked. Rule 2 never runs. You just locked yourself out.

Flip them? Now SSH works from your network. Good.

Pro tip: Put specific rules first (allow from this IP), then general rules (block everyone). Think of it like a bouncer checking a list. Check VIPs first, then run the general rules.

In AWS security groups or Linux iptables, same deal. Order matters big time.

#DevOps #Networking #SecurityGroups #Firewall

Interviewer: "How do you keep secrets safe in GitHub Actions? Like API keys and passwords."

Oh man, people mess this up all the time.

---

Never put secrets in your code or config files. GitHub has a built-in secrets vault.

You store them in Settings > Secrets. Then in your workflow file, you use them like:


env:
  API_KEY: ${{ secrets.MY_API_KEY }}


GitHub masks them in logs so they don't show up when your job runs. But here's the thing: only do this in private repos or with protection rules on.

Better move? Use something like AWS Secrets Manager or HashiCorp Vault. That way your secrets aren't even stored in GitHub. Your Actions job asks the vault "hey, can I have the key?" and it gives it for that one run only.

Real tip: rotate your secrets every few months. And if you ever leak one, delete it right away and make a new one.

#DevOps #GitHubActions #Security #CI-CD

Interviewer: "How do you pass config to a container in Kubernetes?"

This one's important. You've got 3 main ways:

1. ConfigMap — for regular stuff like app settings, db host, etc. Just key-value pairs. Not secret.

2. Secret — same idea but for passwords, api keys, stuff you don't want in plain text.

3. Environment variables — you point to ConfigMap or Secret and boom, your app reads them.

Here's the catch: if you change a ConfigMap, your pod doesn't auto-restart. You gotta manually restart it or use a tool like Sealed Secrets.

Real example:
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: app-config
data:
  DATABASE_HOST: postgres.default
  LOG_LEVEL: info
---
In your pod, mount it:
env:
  - name: DB_HOST
    valueFrom:
      configMapKeyRef:
        name: app-config
        key: DATABASE_HOST

The gotcha: ConfigMaps are NOT encrypted by default. Use Secrets for sensitive stuff.

#Kubernetes #DevOps #ContainerOrchestration #InterviewPrep

Interviewer: "How do you stop bad pods from running in your Kubernetes cluster?"

Nah, this isn't about deleting stuff. It's about setting rules before they even start.

You use something called a policy engine. OPA (Open Policy Agent) is the most common one. It sits between you and Kubernetes and says "yep, that pod is good" or "nope, that breaks the rules."

Example: You set a rule that says "all containers must have resource limits." A developer tries to deploy a pod without limits? OPA blocks it. They get an error telling them why. They fix it. Done.

Why it matters: You catch bad configs before they crash your cluster or cause security issues. It's like a bouncer at the door instead of kicking people out after they're drunk.

Real tip: Start with simple rules. Limit what images you can use, require certain labels, block privileged containers. Don't go crazy with 100 policies on day one.

#Kubernetes #DevOps #OPA #ContainerSecurity #InterviewPrep

Interviewer: "How do you monitor a Kubernetes cluster? What tool would you use?"

Ngl this is asked at like every interview lol


You'd use Prometheus. It scrapes metrics from your pods and nodes every few seconds. Then you can see CPU, memory, and stuff.

Kubernetes exposes a metrics endpoint. Prometheus pulls data from it. Then you set alerts: "if CPU > 80%, tell me."

Prometheus stores the data as time series. You can graph it in Grafana (makes it pretty) or query it yourself.

Real talk: set up alerts BEFORE your app breaks. Don't wait until production melts down.

Example: alert if a pod restarts more than 5 times in 5 min. That's a sign something's wrong.

#Kubernetes #Prometheus #Monitoring #DevOps #ContainerOrchestration

Interviewer: "When would you use Step Functions instead of just writing code?"

Tbh this is a great question. Step Functions let you build workflows without writing complex logic.

Say you need to:
1. Upload a file
2. Check if it's valid
3. Send an email
4. Update a database

You could write all that in one function. But what if step 2 fails? You'd have to restart everything.

With Step Functions, each step is separate. If step 2 fails, you retry just that step. You can see exactly where things broke. Plus you can add delays, parallel tasks, or loop back easily.

Real example: Processing orders. Step 1 checks payment. Step 2 books inventory. Step 3 ships it. If inventory is out of stock, you can automatically notify someone instead of crashing.

It's basically a flowchart that actually runs your AWS services. Way cleaner than spaghetti code.

#AWS #StepFunctions #DevOps #CloudArchitecture

Interviewer: "What's the difference between Helm and just using kubectl?"

Ngl, this one trips people up.

Helm is a package manager for Kubernetes. Think of it like npm for Node or pip for Python.

With kubectl alone, you write YAML files by hand. Every. Single. Time. If you want to deploy the same app to 10 different clusters, you copy-paste and change values. Pain.

Helm packages your app. It has templates. You say "give me 10 copies but change the names and ports" — Helm does it. One command.

Real example: Deploy Nginx with kubectl = write 3 YAML files. Deploy with Helm = helm install nginx nginx-repo/nginx. Done.

Helm also handles upgrades. Need version 2.0? helm upgrade. Old version rolls back automatically if something breaks.

TL;DR: kubectl = manual. Helm = automated and repeatable.

Interviewer: "What's the difference between ECS and Kubernetes? When would you pick one?"

Ngl, this trips people up but it's not hard.

Both run your containers. That's it. Here's the split:

Interviewer: "What's the difference between a service mesh like Istio and just using Kubernetes services?"

Ngl, this one trips people up.


Kubernetes services just route traffic to your pods. That's it. Basic networking.

Istio sits on top and does way more. It watches your traffic, adds security rules, retries failed calls, and can split traffic between versions.

Think of it this way:
- Kubernetes service = basic road signs
- Istio = traffic lights, speed limits, and police directing traffic

You don't *need* Istio for small stuff. But if you're running a bunch of microservices that talk to each other, Istio helps you control who talks to who, retry things that fail, and see what's happening.

Real tip: Istio adds complexity. Don't use it unless you actually need traffic control, security rules between services, or better monitoring. Start simple.

Interviewer: "What's the difference between EC2 Auto Scaling and Karpenter?"

Ngl, people mix these up all the time.

EC2 Auto Scaling watches your CPU and memory. When it goes up, it spins up more servers. When it goes down, it kills servers. It's reactive and slow. Takes a few minutes.

Karpenter is smarter. It watches your pods waiting to run. The second a pod can't fit, Karpenter launches the right server for it. No waiting around.

Big difference: Auto Scaling manages server groups. Karpenter manages individual pods.

Real example: You deploy 50 new pods. Auto Scaling might take 5 mins to notice and launch servers. Karpenter launches them in seconds because it's watching pod events.

Karpenter also picks cheaper servers that fit your needs. Auto Scaling just uses whatever you told it to use.

TL;DR: Auto Scaling is old school. Karpenter is the new way.

#AWS #Kubernetes #Karpenter #DevOps #InterviewPrep

Interviewer: "What's the difference between managing your own Kubernetes cluster vs using Fargate?"

Oh this one gets a lot of people. Let me break it down.

Managing your own cluster? You're running Kubernetes on EC2 servers. You pick the server size, you patch them, you make sure they have enough space. It's powerful but you're doing a lot of work.

Fargate? AWS handles all that for you. You just say "run this container" and it runs. You don't think about servers at all. You pay per second for what you use. Way less headache.

The trade-off: Fargate costs more and you have less control. Own cluster gives you more power but more work.

Pick Fargate when you want things simple and fast. Pick your own cluster when you need total control or you're running tons of stuff and want to save money.

Real talk: most teams start with Fargate. It's less to worry about.

Interviewer: "What's the difference between ConfigMaps and Secrets in Kubernetes?"

this one trips people up ngl


Both store data your app needs. But they're different.

ConfigMaps = store regular stuff. Like database host, app settings, config files. Not secret.

Secrets = store sensitive stuff. Like passwords, API keys, tokens. Kubernetes keeps them separate.

Here's the key part: Secrets are stored as base64 by default (that's just encoding, not real encryption). So don't think they're super safe out of the box. Treat them seriously.

Use ConfigMaps for things your teammates can see. Use Secrets for things they shouldn't.

Quick example: your app needs a database. Store the host in ConfigMap. Store the password in Secret. Your pod reads both.

hook: Interviewer: 'How do you handle pod crashes in Kubernetes?' — Most candidates say 'restart policies' and stop there. Here's what they miss 👇
thread:
Yeah, restart policies help. But here's the real answer:

When a pod crashes, Kubernetes doesn't just restart it randomly. It uses an exponential backoff.

First crash? Restart right away.
Second crash? Wait 10 seconds, then restart.
Third? Wait 20 seconds.
Max wait is 5 minutes.

This prevents hammering your system if the pod keeps failing.

BUT — and this is what gets people — you also need:

1. Liveness probes: Tells Kube 'is this pod actually alive?'
2. Readiness probes: Tells Kube 'is this pod ready for traffic?'
3. Resource requests/limits: So a broken pod doesn't eat all your CPU

Real example: Your app crashes every 2 seconds. Without these checks, Kube keeps spinning up new pods. Your cluster melts down.

With probes? Kube stops sending traffic, waits longer between restarts, and gives you time to fix it.

This is the answer that separates people who just read the docs from people who've actually debugged this stuff.

hook: Interviewer: 'What's the difference between a Deployment and a StatefulSet?' — This one trips up so many engineers. Thread 👇
thread:
OK so here's the thing:

A Deployment is for apps that don't care about order. Like a web server. You need 3 copies running? Kubernetes spins up 3 identical pods. If one dies, it just makes another. Order doesn't matter.

A StatefulSet is for apps that DO care about order. Think databases or messaging systems. Each pod gets a stable name (like db-0, db-1, db-2) and its own storage. Pods start and stop in order. Pod 1 comes up first, then Pod 2, then Pod 3.

Real example: You're running a database cluster. You need Pod 0 to be the leader first. With StatefulSet, that happens. With Deployment, pods might start randomly — total chaos.

Bonus tip: StatefulSets are harder to manage. Use Deployments when you can. Only reach for StatefulSet when your app actually needs it.

hook: Interviewer: 'How do you handle secrets in GitHub Actions?' — Most devs mess this up. Would you? 👇
thread:

env:

hook: Interviewer: 'How would you use CloudFront in your CI/CD pipeline?' — Most engineers miss the real answer. 👇
thread:
CloudFront is a CDN. It caches and delivers your static content fast from servers near your users.

But here's what most people miss in interviews:

CloudFront doesn't run your pipeline. It sits AFTER your pipeline.

Here's the real flow:

1. Your CI/CD pipeline builds your app
2. It uploads static files (images, CSS, JS) to S3
3. CloudFront sits in front of S3
4. Users download from CloudFront, not S3 directly
5. CloudFront caches everything
6. Next user? Lightning fast. No S3 hit.

Why this matters:
- Faster load times for users
- Less load on your servers
- Cheaper (S3 costs less when CloudFront shields it)
- Lower latency globally

One pro tip: Set cache invalidation in your pipeline. After you deploy new files, tell CloudFront to clear old cached versions. Otherwise users see old code.

That's the connection people forget about.

hook: Interviewer: 'What's the difference between Flux and Helm?' — Most candidates mix these up. Here's the truth 👇
thread:
Flux and Helm do different jobs. Don't confuse them.

Helm is a package manager. It bundles your app config into a chart. You run `helm install` and it deploys your stuff once. Done.

Flux is a GitOps tool. It watches your git repo and auto-syncs what's there to your cluster. If you push a change, Flux sees it and applies it. No manual deploy needed.

Real example:
• Helm = You manually ship a box to someone's house
• Flux = You set up a system where any change to your delivery address auto-updates where boxes go

You can actually use them together. Helm creates the chart, Flux watches the repo and deploys it automatically.

hook: Interviewer: 'When would you use Lambda instead of containers?' — Most candidates get this wrong. Here's what they miss 👇
thread:

- Use containers for long-running services

- Lambda costs less if you don't run much. Containers cost the same whether you get 1 request or 1,000

hook: Interviewer: 'How do you know if your app is actually working?' — Most say 'check the logs.' That's not enough. Here's why 👇
thread:
You need metrics. Real numbers. That's where Prometheus comes in.

Prometheus is a tool that watches your app and saves numbers about what it's doing. CPU use. Memory. How many requests came in. How many failed.

Here's the thing most candidates miss:

Logging tells you WHAT went wrong. Metrics tell you WHEN and HOW OFTEN.

Example: Your app crashes at 3am. Logs show an error. But metrics would've shown you the CPU was at 100% for 10 minutes before the crash. You could've fixed it before it broke.

Prometheus stores these metrics as time-series data (just fancy for 'numbers over time'). You set up scrape jobs to pull data from your app every 15 seconds or whatever.

Then you can create alerts: 'If CPU stays above 80% for 5 minutes, wake me up.'

That's the job. Collect metrics. Store them. Alert when bad things happen.

Most engineers know Prometheus exists. But the ones who get hired know HOW to use it — they can explain the difference between a gauge (like temperature) and a counter (like total clicks).

thread:

• You don't want to manage databases. No patching. No backups. AWS does it.
• Your data is simple. Key-value pairs or basic documents.

When NOT to use it:
• Complex joins. If you need data from 5 tables at once, use PostgreSQL instead.
• You need SQL queries. DynamoDB uses a different query language.

Real example: A gaming leaderboard. Player ID → Score. DynamoDB is perfect. Millions of updates per second? No problem.

One tip: Cost. DynamoDB charges per request. If you have a huge database with light traffic, regular SQL might be cheaper.

hook: Interviewer: 'How would you scale pods based on something OTHER than CPU?' — Most candidates get stuck here. Would you? 👇
thread:
This is where KEDA comes in. KEDA = Kubernetes Event Driven Autoscaling.

Normally Kubernetes only scales on CPU or memory. But what if you want to scale based on:

• Message queue depth (RabbitMQ, Kafka)
• HTTP requests per second
• Database connections
• Custom metrics

KEDA lets you do that.

Here's the idea:
KEDA watches an external metric (like your message queue). When the queue gets big, KEDA tells Kubernetes "hey, spin up more pods." When it clears, it scales down.

Real example: Your app processes orders from a queue. You get a spike and 10k messages pile up. KEDA sees it and spins up 20 pods instead of just 2. When the queue clears, it scales back down.

This saves money AND keeps customers happy.

hook: Interviewer: 'What's the difference between Terraform and Flux?' — Most candidates mix these up. Would you nail this? 👇

**Flux** = GitOps tool for Kubernetes. You push changes to Git, Flux watches that repo and automatically updates what's running in your cluster.

Think of it this way:

- Flux keeps your house updated with changes you make (continuous deployment)

Rough example:

- Use Flux to deploy apps INTO that cluster whenever you push code changes to Git

They solve different problems. Terraform = "how do I create infrastructure?" Flux = "how do I automatically sync my apps to what I declared in Git?"

2. Charts — pre-built packages you can reuse
3. Releases — track versions of what you deployed

hook: Interviewer: 'How do you manage Terraform state?' — This trips up 90% of candidates. Would you nail it? 👇
thread:
State is how Terraform knows what's real vs what you wrote.

Think of it like a receipt. You buy stuff, you get a receipt. That receipt is proof of what you own. Terraform's state file = the receipt.

Without it, Terraform doesn't know:
- What you already created
- What changed
- What to delete

HERE'S THE KEY: Never store state locally in a team. Use remote state.

Why? Because:
1. Your laptop crashes = state gone = broke infrastructure
2. Your teammate doesn't see your changes
3. Two people run terraform at once = conflicts

USE THESE: S3 + DynamoDB (AWS), or Terraform Cloud.

S3 stores the file. DynamoDB locks it so only one person can change it at a time. No collisions.

One pro tip: Add state locking to your backend config. It prevents two devs from breaking things together.

hook: Interviewer: 'How do you manage EKS infrastructure with Terraform?' — Most people fumble this. Would you? 👇
thread:
Here's what they want to hear:

You use the aws_eks_cluster and aws_eks_node_group resources. Simple.

BUT — the trick is state management. Your EKS cluster is expensive and takes 10 mins to build. You can't just destroy it by accident.

Here's the real answer:

1. Keep your Terraform state in S3 with versioning ON. If you mess up, you roll back.

2. Use aws_eks_cluster with role_arn pointing to a service role. Never hardcode values.

3. For node groups, use aws_eks_node_group and let it manage the Auto Scaling Group. Don't fight it.

4. Add lifecycle rules. Especially ignore_changes on version during upgrades so Terraform doesn't freak out.

Example:
resource "aws_eks_cluster" "main" {
  name = "my-cluster"
  role_arn = aws_iam_role.eks.arn
  vpc_config {
    subnet_ids = var.subnet_ids
  }
}

That's it. Keep it simple. Most candidates overcomplicate it with modules.

hook: Interviewer: 'How does Route53 handle failover?' — Most engineers get this wrong. Would you? 👇
thread:
Route53 is AWS's DNS service. Think of it like a phone book for the internet.

Failover means: if your main server dies, Route53 automatically points traffic to a backup server instead.

Here's the real answer:

1. You set up health checks. Route53 pings your servers every 30 seconds.

2. If a server stops responding, it's marked as "unhealthy."

3. Route53 stops sending traffic there and sends it to your backup instead.

4. When the main server wakes up, traffic goes back.

Common mistake: Thinking Route53 fixes the broken server. Nope. It just redirects traffic around it.

Real example:
You have a website on Server A (main) and Server B (backup). Route53 checks Server A every 30 seconds. It dies. Route53 sees no response. Boom — all new visitors go to Server B. Your site stays up.

That's it. Not magic. Just smart routing.

hook: Interviewer: 'What's the difference between Karpenter and Cluster Autoscaler?' — Most engineers mix these up. Would you? 👇
thread:
Here's the quick version:

**Cluster Autoscaler**: Old school. Adds nodes when pods can't fit. Slow. Waits for Kubernetes to say "hey, we need space."

**Karpenter**: New hotness. Watches pods BEFORE they fail. Launches the RIGHT node type, RIGHT now. No weird delays.

Real example:

You need a GPU node. With Cluster Autoscaler, your pod sits waiting. Then it times out. Then the scaler notices. Then it adds a node. Pain.

With Karpenter? The pod shows up. Karpenter sees it. Boom. GPU node spins up in seconds. Way smarter.

Karpenter also handles "consolidation" — it notices you have half-empty nodes and packs things better. Saves money.

Bonus: Karpenter works with EC2 spot instances easy. Gets you cheap compute.

TL;DR: Cluster Autoscaler = reactive, slow. Karpenter = proactive, fast, cheaper.

hook: Interviewer: 'When would you use CloudFront instead of just serving from your origin server?' — Most candidates get this wrong. 👇

hook: Interviewer: 'Walk me through your IAM strategy.' — Most engineers panic here. Would you? 👇
thread:
Here's the thing: IAM isn't just about passwords. It's about giving people the LEAST access they need to do their job.

Let's say you have 3 teams:

• Frontend devs — need to push to your container registry
• Backend devs — need database access too
• DevOps team — needs everything

Don't give frontend devs database access. Don't give backend devs power to delete databases. Give each team a role with only what they need.

In AWS or GCP, this means:
- Create roles (frontend-dev, backend-dev, devops-admin)
- Add specific permissions to each role
- Assign people to roles, not permissions directly

It's called "least privilege." It's the golden rule.

Bonus tip: Rotate your keys every 90 days. Old keys sitting around = risk.

hook: Interviewer: 'How is ArgoCD different from regular CI/CD?' — Most engineers mix these up. Do you know? 👇
thread:
ArgoCD isn't about building or testing your code. That's what CI/CD does.

ArgoCD is about DEPLOYING it. It watches your git repo and says: 'Hey, what's in git should match what's running.' If it doesn't match, ArgoCD fixes it.

Example: You push a new app version to git. ArgoCD sees it and auto-deploys to Kubernetes. No manual steps. No scripts.

CI/CD pipeline = build & test code
ArgoCD = keep deployed stuff in sync with git

They work together, not instead of each other. Your CI/CD builds the image. ArgoCD deploys it.

The magic part? If someone manually changes production (bad idea btw), ArgoCD sees the drift and pulls everything back to what git says. It's like version control for your actual running apps.

hook: Interviewer: 'How would you build an internal developer portal?' — Most candidates overthink this. Here's what they miss 👇
thread:
They jump straight to tools. Wrong move.

Start with the PROBLEM: Your devs waste time finding docs, running setup, waiting for access. That's what a portal fixes.

A portal is just one place where devs find:
• How to deploy stuff
• What services exist
• Who owns what
• How to get access

You could build it simple: a wiki + a form for access requests. Or use a tool like Backstage that connects to your GitHub, Jira, and deployment systems.

The KEY insight: Don't pick a tool first. Pick what problems your team has. Then pick the tool that solves them.

Most engineers fail this question because they say 'Backstage' and stop. Real answer is: understand your team first, then build what they need.

hook: Interviewer: 'When would you use Lambda over containers?' — Most candidates get this wrong. Here's what they miss 👇
thread:
Lambda is for SHORT tasks. Containers are for LONG-RUNNING apps. Big difference.

Lambda:
- You write code, AWS runs it
- Pays only when it runs (milliseconds)
- Great for: processing files, handling webhooks, scheduled jobs
- Bad for: 24/7 apps, complex networking

Containers (ECS/EKS):
- You control the whole thing
- Pays even when idle
- Great for: APIs running all day, databases, anything needing persistent state
- Bad for: occasional tasks (too expensive)

Real example: Got a file upload? Lambda processes it in 2 seconds, costs pennies. Got a web app running 24/7? Use containers or EC2.

The trick: Lambda feels cheap until you have HIGH VOLUME tasks. Then you're paying per invocation and it adds up fast.

hook: Interviewer: 'How do you monitor your CI/CD pipeline?' — Most candidates talk about logs. That's not the full picture. 👇
thread:
Here's what they're really asking:

They want to know if you can see WHEN things break in your pipeline, not just IF they break.

Let's say you use Tekton to run your builds. You need to watch:

• How long each step takes
• How many builds fail and why
• Which step fails most
• How long it takes to fix and retry

That's observability. Not just "did it work or not."

A solid answer: "I set up dashboards to track pipeline duration, success rates, and failure points. When a build fails, I can see exactly which step broke and how long it's been stuck. I also get alerts if something's slow or broken."

Bonus: Mention you check both metrics (numbers) and logs (details). Metrics tell you WHAT happened. Logs tell you WHY.

That separates a good SRE from someone who just watches things.

hook: Interviewer: 'What's the difference between monitoring and observability?' — Most candidates mix these up. Would you? 👇
thread:
Monitoring = checking if your app is up. Like pinging a server: 'Hey, are you alive?' Yes or no.

Observability = understanding WHY something broke. You dig into logs, metrics, traces. You ask questions and find answers.

Here's the real difference:

Monitoring watches known things. You set alerts: 'CPU > 80%, page load > 2 seconds.' You already know what to look for.

Observability helps you find unknown problems. Your app crashes and you're lost. But with good logs and traces, you can ask: 'What did this request do? What calls failed? Where did it break?' You figure it out.

Example: Monitoring says 'database is slow.' Observability tells you 'database is slow because this specific query is doing a full table scan on 500k rows.'

One watches the dashboard. One lets you investigate and learn.

Crossplane and other infra tools? Same idea. Monitor your resources. But observe what's actually happening under the hood.

How do you explain this in interviews? Start simple, give an example, then connect it to the job.

hook: Interviewer: 'How would you prevent bad deployments?' — Most candidates miss the actual answer. Thread 👇
thread:
They'll say 'use linting' or 'add tests.' Right, but they're asking about POLICY enforcement.

That's where OPA (Open Policy Agent) comes in.

OPA lets you write rules that block deployments BEFORE they happen. Think of it like a bouncer at the door.

Real example:
- Dev tries to deploy a container with no resource limits
- OPA rule checks: 'Does this have CPU + memory set?'
- If no? Deployment gets blocked. Done.

No resource limits = your pod eats all the server. Bad.

OPA rules are written in a language called Rego. Looks weird at first, but it's just: "if this condition is true, deny the request."

You can use OPA with Kubernetes (via admission controllers), Terraform, or even CI/CD pipelines.

Key wins:
- Catch bad config EARLY (before it reaches prod)
- Same rules everywhere (Kubernetes, Terraform, etc.)
- Teams can't bypass it (it's enforced at the platform level)

Common OPA policies:
- Must have resource requests/limits
- Only certain image registries allowed
- Containers must run as non-root
- Storage must be encrypted

If they ask this in your interview, mention OPA + one specific policy example. You'll stand out.

hook: Interviewer: 'How do you track which services are down?' — Most candidates miss the obvious answer. Here's what they should say 👇
thread:
The answer: You need a way to SEE your services. That's monitoring + alerting.

Here's the real flow:

1. Your app sends metrics (CPU, memory, errors)
2. A tool stores them (Prometheus, Datadog, etc)
3. You set alerts ("if errors > 10%, page me")
4. When it hits, you get notified

Tools like Backstage help here. It's a dashboard. Shows ALL your services in one place. One tab tells you which ones are broken.

Why this matters: You can't fix what you can't see. Without monitoring, you're blind.

Example: Your payment service crashes at 2am. With monitoring, an alert wakes you up in 30 seconds. Without it? Your customers find out first. Bad.

Bonus tip: Don't just monitor uptime. Watch these too:
- Response time (is it slow?)
- Error rate (is it broken?)
- Database queries (are they piling up?)

hook: Interviewer: 'How do you monitor infrastructure defined in Terraform?' — Most candidates miss the real answer. 👇
thread:
Here's the thing: Terraform creates your infrastructure, but it doesn't watch it.

You need observability OUTSIDE of Terraform. Here's what works:

1. **Prometheus** - scrapes metrics from your servers and apps every 15 seconds. You see CPU, memory, disk.

2. **CloudWatch** (AWS) or **Stackdriver** (GCP) - these watch the actual cloud resources Terraform built. They track if your database is slow or your load balancer fails.

3. **Logs** - use something like Loki or ELK Stack. Your apps write logs. You read them to find problems.

The trick? Use Terraform to BUILD the monitoring too. Write Terraform code that sets up Prometheus scrape configs. Set up CloudWatch alarms WITH Terraform. That way, when you deploy new apps, monitoring deploys automatically.

Example: Your Terraform creates an EC2 instance. It also creates a CloudWatch alarm that alerts you if that instance's CPU stays above 80% for 5 minutes. Both happen at once.

hook: Interviewer: 'How does Karpenter differ from the Kubernetes autoscaler?' — Most engineers mix these up. Would you? 👇
thread:
Here's the thing: the Kubernetes autoscaler (Cluster Autoscaler) adds nodes when pods can't fit. It's reactive.

Karpenter is faster and smarter. It watches your pods BEFORE they get stuck. It can spin up nodes in seconds, not minutes.

Real example:

With Cluster Autoscaler: Pod sits pending → autoscaler notices → adds node → pod runs (slow)

With Karpenter: Pod comes in → Karpenter sees it → node already starting → pod runs fast

Bonus: Karpenter is also way better at bin-packing. It fits more pods per node so you waste less money.

One more thing — Karpenter talks directly to your cloud provider (AWS, Azure, GCP). Cluster Autoscaler is more generic.

So in interviews, say this: "Karpenter is faster, smarter about resource use, and costs less. Cluster Autoscaler is simpler but slower."

hook: Interviewer: 'Why would you put an API Gateway in front of your microservices?' — Most candidates miss the real reason. 👇
thread:
Here's what people usually say: 'It routes requests.' True, but boring.

The REAL reason: An API Gateway is your traffic cop. It sits between your users and your services. It can:

• Stop bad requests before they hit your servers
• Rate limit (stop someone from hammering your API)
• Add auth checks (verify they should be here)
• Log everything that comes in
• Route to different versions of your service

Example: Without a gateway, each microservice has to do its own security. With one? You do it once, in one place. Way simpler.

Think of it like airport security. You don't want security at every gate. One checkpoint handles it all.

Bonus tip: Popular ones are Kong, AWS API Gateway, NGINX. Know at least one by name in your interview.

hook: Interviewer: 'How do buildpacks fit into your CI/CD pipeline?' — Most candidates mix this up with Docker. Would you nail it? 👇
thread:
Here's the thing: buildpacks are just smart shortcuts.

Instead of writing a Dockerfile yourself, a buildpack looks at your code and says "oh, this is a Node app" — then it builds everything automatically.

Real example:
You push code to Heroku or Cloud Foundry. The platform runs a buildpack. It detects your language, installs deps, bundles your app into a container. Done.

Why it matters:
- Faster. You skip writing Dockerfiles
- Safer. Less mistakes because the buildpack knows best practices
- Portable. Same buildpack works on different platforms

Docker vs Buildpacks:
Docker = you control everything (good if you want that)
Buildpacks = convention over config (good if you just want it working)

They're not enemies. Modern buildpacks actually CREATE Docker images behind the scenes.

In an interview, just say: "Buildpacks automate container builds by detecting your app type and applying best practices. We use them to speed up our CI/CD without maintaining Dockerfiles."

hook: Interviewer: 'What's the difference between SNS and SQS?' — This one trips up SO many engineers. Would you nail it? 👇
thread:
Here's the easy way to remember it:

SNS = a megaphone. You shout once, everyone listening hears it. It's a broadcast.

SQS = a mailbox. Messages sit there. One person reads one message at a time.

Real example:

SNS: Alert goes out "Server is down!" All teams get it right away.

SQS: Order comes in. It waits in the queue. One worker picks it up, processes it, then moves on.

Key difference?
- SNS = one-to-many, real-time, doesn't wait
- SQS = one-to-one (or batches), queued up, decoupled

Bonus tip: You can use them together. SNS sends a message, SQS catches it and stores it. Best of both worlds.

hook: Interviewer: 'How would you detect suspicious activity in AWS?' — Most people say CloudTrail and stop. But there's a better answer 👇
thread:
Yeah, CloudTrail logs everything. But it's like having a camera that just records — you still need someone watching it.

That's where GuardDuty comes in. It's AWS's security service that actually WATCHES your logs for you.

Here's the real difference:

🔹 CloudTrail = Records what happened
🔹 GuardDuty = Finds the bad stuff in those records

GuardDuty uses machine learning to spot weird patterns. Like:
- Someone logging in from 10 countries in 1 hour
- Tons of failed login attempts
- Data being downloaded to an unusual place
- Cryptocurrency mining activity

It costs way less than hiring a security team to read logs all day.

Pro tip for interviews: Say you'd use BOTH together. CloudTrail for the record. GuardDuty for the alarm. That shows you get the full picture.
